title: Wedge Drop
teaches: The Wedge Drop as we use it: a bounce makes a top, stalls a few days on Kell's fast averages, then closes down through them. For every long holder it is the sell signal. It is a short only in the narrow form below the 200-day, in a weak market: short as price trades down through the trigger, never at the close, the stop a few cents over the trigger day's high within about 3%, the first cover is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, the rest on the trail, and a close back above both averages is the exit. We recommend shorting only to traders who have already made $1 million.

facts.quote: The Wedge Drop happens when the market trades back below the moving averages after a strong rally, known as an Exhaustion Extension.
facts.claim: TraderLion: the Wedge Drop is the trade back below the moving averages after a strong rally.

facts.quote: After an Exhaustion Extension, prices often trade in a tight range as moving averages catch up.
facts.claim: TraderLion: after the extension, price trades in a tight range while the averages catch up.

facts.quote: Sometimes, you won’t see a big Exhaustion Extension, but the price will trade sideways and eventually lose momentum.
facts.claim: TraderLion: a Wedge Drop can come without a big extension, out of sideways trade.

facts.quote: If you’re sitting on gains from an earlier entry, use the Wedge Drop as a signal to protect profits and reduce exposure.
facts.claim: TraderLion: for a long holder the Wedge Drop is the signal to protect profits.

facts.quote: As the price breaks below moving averages with increased selling pressure, you can enter a short position with a stop just above the recent high.
facts.claim: TraderLion: the short enters as price breaks below the averages on selling pressure, stop above the recent high.

facts.quote: If the stock regains its moving averages and pushes higher, exit the short position.
facts.claim: TraderLion: if the stock regains its averages, exit the short.

facts.quote: It’s also best to avoid shorting early in new bull markets or strong uptrending stocks.
facts.claim: TraderLion: avoid shorting early in new bull markets or strong uptrending stocks.

facts.quote: So when an index like the S&P 500 or Nasdaq forms a Wedge Drop, it’s a warning that the market as a whole is weakening.
facts.claim: TraderLion: an index Wedge Drop warns that the whole market is weakening.

facts.quote: When several leaders fall below their moving averages in a Wedge Drop pattern, it’s a sign to get defensive.
facts.claim: TraderLion: several leaders in Wedge Drops is a sign to get defensive.

facts.quote: For more aggressive traders, the Wedge Drop can also be an opportunity to go short.
facts.claim: TraderLion: the short is for more aggressive traders.

facts.quote: If you’re more aggressive, shorting can be a good play, but you’ll need to set tight stop-losses and be aware of rising volatility as the stock trends lower.
facts.claim: TraderLion: the short needs tight stops and rising volatility as the stock falls.

facts.quote: Decreased buying volume (accumulation)
facts.claim: TraderLion lists decreased buying volume among the warning signs before the drop.

facts.quote: Increased selling volume (distribution)
facts.claim: TraderLion lists increased selling volume among the warning signs before the drop.

facts.quote: After the Exhaustion Extension, the price will trade tight into the moving averages as there are now fewer new buyers.
facts.claim: Kell's cycle page: after the extension, price trades tight into the averages.

facts.quote: The Wedge Drop confirms the reversal when the price falls through the moving averages with an influx of sellers.
facts.claim: Kell's cycle page: the Wedge Drop is price falling through the averages with an influx of sellers.

facts.quote: 10 and 20-day exponential moving averages guide us through the intermediate-term trend
facts.claim: Kell's pair is the 10 and 20-day exponential moving averages.

facts.quote: Like an EMA Crossback to the upside, an EMA Crossback to the downside will retest the moving averages but is now met with more resistance, pushing the stock lower.
facts.claim: Kell: after the drop, a downside EMA Crossback retests the averages and is met with resistance.

facts.quote: If a stock tops and starts to decline, step aside and let the cycle reset before jumping back in.
facts.claim: Kell's cycle page: once a stock tops, step aside and let the cycle reset.

facts.quote: Hourly and 15-minute charts are for timing entries.
facts.claim: Kell: hourly and 15-minute charts are for timing entries.

facts.quote: Downtrends are volatile, and ideally, any long positions have been closed at the Wedge Drop.

facts.quote: Be careful not to short too late in the downtrend, just like buying late in an uptrend.

facts.claim: A lower-high top peaks under the highest high of the 60 sessions before it.

facts.claim: The stall runs 3 to 10 sessions from the top to the trigger day.

facts.quote: Through the stall no close is more than 1 ATR from the 10-day EMA.
facts.claim: In the stall no close sits more than 1 ATR from the 10-day EMA.

facts.quote: No new high in the last 3 sessions of the stall.
facts.claim: No new high in the stall's last 3 sessions.

facts.quote: In the stall the up days come on lighter volume than the down days.
facts.claim: In the stall the up days are lighter than the down days.

facts.quote: Wide, loose action before the drop is graded down, not excluded.
facts.claim: Wide, loose action before the drop is graded down, not excluded.

facts.quote: The trigger day closes in the lower 40% of its range.
facts.claim: The trigger day closes in the lower 40% of its range.

facts.quote: Advanced: an intraday break of the stall low on the 65-minute chart counts only once the daily close confirms it.

facts.claim: No adding at the crossback; it is a new trade with its own stop.

facts.quote: A close above the trigger day's high: the stop has already gone; the stop is the exit.

questions.q: What just happened on the last bar?
choices: It closed down through both averages
It closed under the 200-day
It retested both averages from below
It closed up through both averages
questions.answer: It closed down through both averages
questions.why: It closed down through both averages. That's the Wedge Drop. META had been sitting tight on those lines because fewer new buyers were showing up. Today sellers pushed it through both in one day, on heavy volume. That's your tell that sellers have taken over. If you're long, that's your sell. It's no short though. META's still way above a rising 200-day.
questions.lesson_line: A run, a tight rest on the averages, then a close down through them. That's the drop.

wrong.It closed under the 200-day: Not even close. META's way above its 200-day. The drop is the close through the two short averages.
wrong.It retested both averages from below: That's the crossback, and it comes after a drop. Here price fell through the averages it was resting on.
wrong.It closed up through both averages: That's the Wedge Pop, the mirror. It comes from under the averages and closes up through them.

questions.simple: It closed down through both averages. Sellers just took over from the buyers who had been holding it up.

reasons: fixed before (cold check)

questions.story: This stock sat for a few days right on its two short averages, the 9 and 20 EMA. The chart ends on today's bar. Watch where it closes.

deeper.counter: Kell puts it this way: the Wedge Drop confirms the reversal when price falls through the averages with an influx of sellers.

questions.q: A stock well above its 200-day just closed down through both EMAs. For us, that's a sell signal, not a short.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Above the 200-day we don't short stocks. That's a hard line. The one exception is a parabolic short on its climax day, and a quiet drop through the EMAs isn't that. The drop still matters, though. If you own it, sell. In our own scan the plain Wedge Drop had no edge by itself. It only showed an edge with the stock under its 200-day and the market under its 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day it tells you to sell. Only below it can it be a short.
questions.simple: True. Above the 200-day the bigger trend is still up, so we sell our long there but we don't short it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B26, a hard rule)

questions.q: What came right before today's drop?
choices: A run up, then a tight stall
A long base, then a breakout
A steady slide with no pause
A gap up out of a flat base
questions.answer: A run up, then a tight stall
questions.why: A run up, then a tight stall. That's the usual order. AAPL ran into the summer, then sat tight on its averages through July while they caught up. Price goes quiet there because fewer new buyers are showing up. Then sellers push it through. You won't always get a big run first. Sometimes it just goes sideways and runs out of steam. Either way, the rest on the averages comes before the drop.
questions.lesson_line: First the run, then the rest on the averages, then the drop. Learn the order.

wrong.A steady slide with no pause: A drop comes out of a rest. AAPL paused tight on its averages first.
wrong.A gap up out of a flat base: That's a breakout buy. A drop follows a top, not a breakout.
wrong.A long base, then a breakout: That's a long setup. The rest before a drop is days on the averages, not months.

questions.simple: A run up, then a tight rest on the averages. Fewer new buyers show up, and then sellers push it through.
questions.story: This stock ran hard into the summer, then went sideways on its short averages through July. The chart ends on the day it closed under both.

deeper.example: TraderLion: after an Exhaustion Extension, prices often trade in a tight range as the moving averages catch up. Sometimes there's no big extension, just sideways trade that loses momentum.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: No short more than ___% under the trigger level.
questions.why: 4%. We never short more than 4% under the trigger level. It mirrors our no-chase line for longs, 4% past the buy point, because shorts are our long setups reversed. Past 4%, we skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Four percent under the trigger and I am done. I would rather miss it than chase it.
questions.simple: The limit is 4%. If the price is already more than 4% under the trigger level, we skip the short.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, mirrored by D47)

questions.q: Your short got covered on a reclaim. The next day it closes back under both EMAs. That's a fresh short.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. One close back under isn't a setup. The reclaim just showed you that buyers can take those averages back. Before I short it again, I want a new rest on the averages, quiet days where the buying dries up. Then a new close down through them. That's a brand new trade with its own stop. Shorting the first wiggle back under is how you get chopped up twice.
questions.lesson_line: Once it fails, the next short needs a whole new setup. Not just one more close under.
questions.simple: False. The reclaim showed buyers are still around, so a second short needs a new stall and a new drop first.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Where's your stop on this short?
choices: A few cents over today's high
A few cents under today's low
A few cents over the 200-day
Right on today's high
questions.answer: A few cents over today's high
questions.why: A few cents over today's high. On a short you lose when price goes up, so the stop sits above you. The trigger day's high is the closest spot where the idea is clearly wrong. Trade back over it and sellers didn't take over after all. Put it a few cents past the high, not right on it. I want 1 to 3%, and I'll take up to 5%. One honest thing on this chart. It closed only a hair under a flat 200-day. That's barely a short, so it grades lower and the size comes down.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first. A few cents over the trigger day's high, then check the distance.

wrong.A few cents under today's low: That's where a long's stop goes. On a short your risk is above you.
wrong.A few cents over the 200-day: The 200-day decides if you can short at all. It's not where the stop goes.
wrong.Right on today's high: Right on the high gets tagged by one tick. Give it a few cents.

questions.simple: Over today's high. A short loses when price goes up, and a move back over that high means you're wrong.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-008, where the stop goes)

questions.story: The chart ends on the trigger day, the day it broke down through both EMAs. You're short.

questions.q: On our card the stall runs 3 to 10 sessions between the top and the trigger day.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The card says the stall runs 3 to 10 sessions between the top and the trigger day. Those numbers are the card's, not Kell's. He only says that after the extension, price trades tight into the moving averages as there are fewer new buyers.
questions.lesson_line: Three to ten days of rest on the averages. Then the close decides.
questions.simple: True. Our card gives the stall three to ten sessions between the top and the trigger day.

reasons: rests on a proposed card number

questions.q: What is that a warning of?
choices: The whole market is weakening
Only a few big stocks are tired
A pause before the next leg up
A buy point for the market leaders
questions.answer: The whole market is weakening
questions.why: The market as a whole is weakening. TraderLion: when an index like the S&P 500 or Nasdaq forms a Wedge Drop, it is a warning. Several leaders in Wedge Drops is a sign to get defensive. Bracco read the Nasdaq's drop as the start of another leg down. The chart is QQQ in a bear market: a bounce made a lower high and then dropped, and the lows over the next weeks sat well under the trigger close.
questions.lesson_line: An index Wedge Drop is a warning for the whole market, not just one stock.

wrong.A buy point for the market leaders: Several leaders in Wedge Drops is a sign to get defensive, not to buy.
wrong.Only a few big stocks are tired: TraderLion: an index Wedge Drop warns that the market as a whole is weakening, not a few names.
wrong.A pause before the next leg up: Bracco read the Nasdaq's drop as the start of another leg down. Kell read an index drop as confirmation of a deeper pullback.

questions.simple: A Wedge Drop in the index warns that the whole market is getting weaker, not just one stock.

deeper.example: Kell dated this on QQQ: an Exhaustion Extension on 2/2, a Wedge Drop on 2/16 and 2/17, an EMA Crossback on 2/23. That index drop sat above the 200-day, so for us it was a sell signal for longs, not a short.

reasons: a card rule, proposed

questions.story: Hidden index fund, the trigger day is the last bar. The index itself forms a Wedge Drop.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: A short still under 1R of profit after ___ sessions is covered.
questions.why: 10. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is closed, which frees the money. For a short, closed means covered.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and nothing. The money has somewhere better to be.
questions.simple: After 10 trading days with less than 1R of profit, we cover the short and free the money for something better.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, the time stop)

questions.q: Before the trigger day, how many of the last 10 closes must sit above the 20-day EMA on our card?
choices: At least 5
At least 7
At least 8
At least 9
questions.answer: At least 8
questions.why: At least 8 of the 10. The card wants at least 8 of the 10 closes before the trigger day above the 20-day EMA. That is the prior bounce. For a short, Kell drew it as a fast rally in a bear market. It puts in a lower high and then drops. A dip under the 20-day is allowed, so it does not need all 10. The 8 is the card's proposed number.
questions.lesson_line: No bounce, no drop. Eight of the last ten closes over the 20-day EMA is the bounce.

wrong.At least 5: Five of ten is only half the closes. The card wants eight.
wrong.At least 7: Seven of ten falls short. The card wants eight.
wrong.At least 9: Nine is stricter than the card. A dip under the 20-day is allowed, and eight of ten is the line.

questions.simple: At least 8 of the last 10 closes must sit above the 20-day average. That is what makes it a bounce.

reasons: rests on a proposed card number
tied to a held decision (D-021)

questions.story: The stock has an RS rating of 92 and leads its group. It stalls four days on its averages, then closes under them, under the 200-day.
questions.q: Short it?
choices: No; a leader, not the weakest
Yes; it closed under the averages
Yes; RS does not matter on shorts
questions.answer: No; a leader, not the weakest
questions.why: No. Shorts are the mirror: the weakest stocks, an RS rating of 20 or less, in the weakest groups. A leader with strong RS is the B- row, and TraderLion says to avoid strong uptrending stocks.
questions.lesson_line: Short the weakest, not the strongest. A leader that lost its averages once is not weak.

wrong.Yes; it closed under the averages: The close is one gate. The RS rule is another, and a 92 fails it.
wrong.Yes; RS does not matter on shorts: It matters in mirror image: 20 or less, in a weak group.

questions.q: A $6 stock trading $3 million a day just gave a picture-perfect Wedge Drop. It's a short you can take.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. I'd never touch it. We only trade stocks at $10 or more that trade at least $20 million a day. This one is $6 and $3 million, so it fails both. Thin stocks jump around on small orders. On a short that's worse, because a squeeze can run straight through your stop and you can't get out clean. A pretty chart doesn't fix that.
questions.lesson_line: Liquidity first, chart second. Under $10 or under $20 million a day, it's not on the list.
questions.simple: False. It's too thin to get in and out of, and we only trade $10 stocks doing $20 million a day.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B23)

questions.q: You're long. It ran, you didn't sell into the push, and today it closed down through both EMAs. What do you do?
choices: Sell, the drop is your exit
Wait to sell on the crossback
Hold, a Wedge Pop comes next
Hold until it loses the 200-day
questions.answer: Sell, the drop is your exit
questions.why: Sell. The Wedge Drop is your last exit on a long. Ideally you sold some into the run. If you didn't, the drop is the backstop that takes you out with most of the gain. Holding through it and hoping is how a good trade turns into a round trip. If it turns out to be a shakeout, fine. You buy it back on a new setup.
questions.lesson_line: The drop is the last exit for a long. Not a reason to hope.

wrong.Wait to sell on the crossback: The crossback comes after the drop, at a worse price. Longs should be out at the drop.
wrong.Hold, a Wedge Pop comes next: A pop is a buy setup from under the averages. Waiting for one means riding the whole fall.
wrong.Hold until it loses the 200-day: By then most of the gain is gone. The drop is the exit, and the 200-day is far too late.

questions.simple: Sell. The drop is the last exit on a long, and you can always buy back on a new setup.

deeper.counter: Kell says it plainly. If you don't sell the second extension or it doesn't come, allow the Wedge Drop to protect you and take you out.

questions.q: You don't open a new short in the 3 days before the company reports earnings.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. We open nothing new in the 3 days before a report, long or short. The reason is the gap. A report can open the stock right over your stop overnight, and a stop can't catch a gap. You'd take a loss way bigger than you planned. Let the report pass, then look for a fresh trigger. A short you already hold only stays through it if it's up 5R.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings in 3 days or less, no new short. Let the report pass first.
questions.simple: True. A report can gap the stock right past your stop, so no new short in the 3 days before it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22)

questions.q: In the stall, how far may a close sit from the 9 EMA on our card?
choices: No more than 0.5 ATR
No more than 1 ATR
No more than 2 ATR
No more than 5%
questions.answer: No more than 1 ATR
questions.why: No more than 1 ATR. Through the stall no close is more than 1 ATR from the 9 EMA. ATR is the stock's own usual daily range, so the test fits each stock. Kell: price trades tight into the moving averages. The 1 ATR is the card's proposed number.
questions.lesson_line: The stall hugs the 9 EMA. Far from it is not a stall.

wrong.No more than 5%: The stall test is set in ATR, the stock's own usual daily range, not in a fixed percent.
wrong.No more than 0.5 ATR: That is stricter than the card. The line is 1 ATR.
wrong.No more than 2 ATR: Too loose. The card's line is 1 ATR from the 9 EMA.

questions.simple: No close in the stall sits more than one typical day's range away from the 9 EMA.

reasons: rests on a proposed card number
tied to a held decision (D-021)

questions.story: A bear market, and the stock sits under a falling 200-day. A bounce runs into its falling averages, turns down under its earlier high, then stalls four days.
questions.q: What kind of top did it just make?
choices: A lower high, the bear-market top
An extension far over the 20 EMA
A failed push past yesterday's high
No top yet, just a pause
questions.answer: A lower high, the bear-market top
questions.why: A lower high. The bounce never got back to the old high. It got turned away at the falling averages instead. That's the picture I want for a short. Under the 200-day, a decent pop back up, then a rejection near the 50-day or 20 EMA. Buyers tried and ran out of gas below the last peak. When it drops, your stop goes a few cents over the trigger day's high.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day, a pop that fails at the falling averages. That's the short I want.

wrong.An extension far over the 20 EMA: An extension is a close stretched way above the 20 EMA. This bounce barely reached its averages.
wrong.A failed push past yesterday's high: That's one day failing to clear the day before. This whole bounce peaked under the earlier high.
wrong.No top yet, just a pause: A bounce that turns under the old high and stalls is the top. The drop then confirms it.

questions.simple: A lower high. The bounce failed below the old peak at falling averages, so buyers are getting weaker.

deeper.example: WHR in a bear market: the bounce made a lower high at the falling 20 EMA and stalled four days. The next day it closed under both averages, and the averages led it lower.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: A stock makes a new high Monday, then closes under both EMAs Tuesday. That's a Wedge Drop.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. There was no rest. A Wedge Drop needs a stall first, a few quiet days on the averages with no new high. A stock making a new high the day before still has buyers. Short that and you're shorting a leader at its highs, and the stop over the high gets taken fast. Wait. If it stalls, goes quiet and then breaks, now you've got something.
questions.lesson_line: No stall, no drop. Wait for the quiet days first.
questions.simple: False. A stock still making new highs has buyers, so there's no stall and no drop to short yet.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: Everything checks out: the stall, the averages, the 200-day. But the trigger day gaps down and opens 12% under the 9 EMA.
questions.q: Do you short it at the open?
choices: Pass, it's 12% under the 9 EMA
Pass, the stall was too short
Short it, the gap confirms the top
Short it at half size, same stop
questions.answer: Pass, it's 12% under the 9 EMA
questions.why: Pass. Opening 12% under the 9 EMA, most of the quick move is already done. Shorting here is chasing, just in the other direction. We skip a long that's more than 10% over its 9 EMA, and a short is the same rule flipped. Stretched like that, a snap back up toward the average can hit your stop before the drop does any work. Let it go.
questions.lesson_line: A stretched drop is still a chase. Let it go and wait for the next one.

wrong.Pass, the stall was too short: The story says the stall checked out. The problem is how stretched it opened.
wrong.Short it, the gap confirms the top: The gap does confirm it. It also puts the short too far from the average to chase.
wrong.Short it at half size, same stop: Smaller size doesn't fix a chase. Skip it.

questions.simple: Pass. It opened way too far under its 9 EMA, so shorting now chases a move that's mostly done.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C29, mirrored by D47)

questions.q: When do you make your first cover?
choices: Day 3 or later, into a push
Day 1, lock in the quick gain
At exactly 3R, whatever the day
Never, hold it all to the end
questions.answer: Day 3 or later, into a push
questions.why: Day 3 or later, into a push. The first cover is a judgment call, not a fixed third at 3R. We very rarely sell on day 1. I want to cover into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, or around 5 to 10R. That's where the move gives you something to sell into. EXP hit 3R by day 3 and kept going. Covering on day 1 would have left most of that on the table.
questions.lesson_line: Rarely cover on day 1. Day 3 at the earliest, into a push.

wrong.At exactly 3R, whatever the day: 3R isn't an order. The first cover is a judgment, often into a push of several days.
wrong.Day 1, lock in the quick gain: We very rarely sell on day 1. That cuts the winner before it's had a chance to move.
wrong.Never, hold it all to the end: We do cover. Some comes off into strength, and the trail handles the rest.

questions.simple: Day 3 or later. We cover into a push of several days, not on day 1, so the winner gets room.

reasons: rests on the owner's ruling D-013 (the first sell is a judgment)
the short side mirrors the long side (D47)

questions.story: You shorted this one on the trigger day. It's working, sliding away from your entry.

questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: About 2.03%. The stop is 1.12 above a 55.16 fill, right inside the range we like.

reasons: +2 a computed key
+1 fixed before

wrong.1.12%: That's the gap in dollars, 1.12. You still have to divide it by the fill.
wrong.20.3%: A decimal slip, one place too far right. 1.12 is a small slice of 55.16.

questions.story: A bear market. You shorted the trigger day at 55.16 with the stop at 56.28, a few cents over the day's high.
You're short from 24.74 with the stop at 25.26. Two days later it closes back above both EMAs. Your stop hasn't been hit.
questions.q: It just took back both averages. What's the play?
choices: Cover, the reclaim is the exit
Hold, the stop is still above it
Add, it's a better price now
Move the stop to breakeven
questions.answer: Cover, the reclaim is the exit
questions.why: Cover. A close back above both averages takes away the reason you're short. You shorted because sellers pushed it through those lines. Now buyers took them back. You don't need to wait for the stop. DIS did this on day 2, and the stop didn't get hit until the earnings reaction day. Covering on the reclaim cost a lot less. If you want back in later, that needs a new stall and a new drop.
questions.lesson_line: The reclaim cancels the drop. Cover, and wait for a new stall.

wrong.Move the stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes once the trade has paid, between 2R and 5R. This one is going the wrong way.
wrong.Hold, the stop is still above it: The stop is your last line, not your only exit. The reclaim already told you the trade is broken.
wrong.Add, it's a better price now: Adding to a broken short makes it worse. Full size at one price, one stop, and never add to a loser.

questions.simple: Cover. Buyers took back both averages, so the reason for the short is gone.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
fixed before (cold check)

deeper.counter: TraderLion's page says the same: if the stock regains its moving averages and pushes higher, exit the short position.

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Cover the last third on a close back above the 10-day EMA for a fast mover, the ___-day for a steadier one.
questions.why: 21. Our default trail is the 10-day average for fast movers and the 21-day for steadier ones. We cover the last third on a close back above it, not on a touch. Kell expects a retest of the averages after the drop to meet resistance.
questions.lesson_line: Trail the falling average. Cover the close back above it, not the touch.
questions.simple: The steadier movers use the 21-day average. We cover the last third on a close back above it.

deeper.trap: A rally that stalls under the falling averages is a place to hold, not to panic. The trail covers only on a close back above the 10-day or 21-day. A poke above it that fades by the close is not a cover.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)

questions.q: At what price is the trade up 2R?
questions.why: $44.10. One R is 46.89 minus 45.96, the risk on each share. On a short you make money as price falls, so you count down from your fill. One R down gets you to 45.03. Two R down is 44.10. Somewhere from 2R to 5R, or at your first sell, I'll pull the stop down to breakeven. From there the trade can't turn into a loser. PCG got to 3R on day 10.
questions.lesson_line: Know where 2R sits. From there to 5R, moving the stop to breakeven is your call.
questions.simple: $44.10. Take twice the stop distance off your fill, since a short makes money as price falls.

reasons: a computed key
the first cover is the owner's D-013 judgment, not a fixed 3R cover

wrong.$44.10: Right: two stop distances below the fill.
wrong.$45.03: That's only one stop distance below your fill.
wrong.$47.82: That's two stop distances above your fill. On a short, the profit is below.

A textbook stall breaks under both averages in a stock under its 200-day. The app's market filter reads Green: the index is in an uptrend and the account trades longs at full risk.
questions.q: What is your call?
choices: No short; Green is for longs
Buy the dip; the market is Green
Short; the stock is under its 200
Short, but at half size only
questions.answer: No short; Green is for longs
questions.why: No short. Green means the account trades at full risk, and that is a long's market. The reading is a guide, but our shorts are the weak market's trade. In Red we hold mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day. Being under the 200-day is one gate, not the only one. In our scan the drop separated from the base rate only in a market under its 50-day. For a long holder this is still a sell signal.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market before the stock. A short in a Green market is a fight you picked.

wrong.Short; the stock is under its 200: The 200-day is the stock's gate. The market reading is another, and Green fails it.
wrong.Buy the dip; the market is Green: No longs below the 200-day, and a Wedge Drop tells a long holder to sell.
wrong.Short, but at half size only: Size does not fix the market. In a Green market a short is still a fight against the filter.

questions.simple: No short. Green is a long's market, and our shorts come in a weak market, not a strong one.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-023, the market filter)
+1 fixed before

questions.story: The trigger day is the last bar. The stock closes under both averages after a clean stall. But the close sits at 56% of the day's range, mid-bar.
questions.q: Is that the trigger?
choices: No; it must close in the lower 40%
Yes; any close under both averages works
Yes, if volume was heavy that day
No; it must close at the day's low
questions.answer: No; it must close in the lower 40%
questions.why: No. The trigger day closes in the lower 40% of its range. This one closed at 56%. A mid-range close under the averages is undecided, so wait for the next close. LOW 2007-09-07 closed at 56% and was a near miss.
questions.lesson_line: Where the day closes is the vote. Mid-range is no vote.

wrong.Yes; any close under both averages works: A close under both is the event, not the whole trigger. The day must also close in the lower 40% of its range.
wrong.Yes, if volume was heavy that day: Volume is not the test here. Where the day closes in its range is.
wrong.No; it must close at the day's low: The card asks for the lower 40% of the range, not the exact low. A close near the low counts.

questions.simple: No. The day has to close in the lower 40% of its range, and a close near the middle has not decided anything.

deeper.counter: The card does not say a mid-range close can never work. It says the vote is not in yet. In one case, LOW closed at 56% of its range, and it stayed a near miss.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: In the stall, what does our card want from the volume?
choices: Up days lighter than down days
Up days heavier than down days
Up and down days on equal volume
Volume rising on every day
questions.answer: Up days lighter than down days
questions.why: Up days lighter than down days. The card wants the up days in the stall on lighter volume than the down days. Kell: price trades tight into the moving averages as there are now fewer new buyers.
questions.lesson_line: Quiet up days, heavier down days. Fewer new buyers while price rests on the averages.

wrong.Up days heavier than down days: That is buyers stepping in, not fading. The card wants the up days lighter.
wrong.Up and down days on equal volume: The card wants the up days lighter than the down days, not equal.
wrong.Volume rising on every day: The stall wants quiet up days. Rising volume every day is not a rest.

questions.simple: In a stall, up days trade on lighter volume than down days. That fits fewer new buyers.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.q: Shorted at 78.94, stop 80.77. The stock trades down to 69.79. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5.0R. One R is the stop minus the fill: 80.77 - 78.94. The gain is the fill minus the price: 78.94 - 69.79. Gain over R: (78.94 - 69.79) / (80.77 - 78.94) = 5.0. That is a measure, not a fixed cover price. EXP reached 3R in three sessions on the way.
questions.lesson_line: Count a short in R too. The gain divided by one R is the R.
questions.simple: The fall from the fill is 5.0 times the stop distance, so it is 5.0R.

reasons: a computed key
when to cover is the owner's D-013 judgment

wrong.0.2R: Flipped the division: one R over the gain.
wrong.0.1R: Divided the gain by the price, not by R.
wrong.1.8R: That is one R in dollars read as R. Divide the gain by it.

questions.story: Shorted on the trigger day.
You're short from 36.65 with the stop at 37.22. Overnight it gaps up and opens at 37.40, over your stop. The first 30-minute bar runs from 37.05 to 37.55.
questions.q: Where's your stop now?
choices: 37.55, the first 30-minute high
37.05, the first 30-minute low
37.40, the opening price
Cover now, the gap is past 2R
questions.answer: 37.55, the first 30-minute high
questions.why: 37.55, the high of the first 30 minutes. A stop can't catch an overnight gap, so 37.22 is already behind you. It's the one time a stop moves wider. Let the first 30 minutes show you where price settles. On a short, the high of that bar is your new stop. There's a ceiling, though. If those 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, you're out. Here they don't, so you hold with the new stop.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop is the one exception. The first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.37.05, the first 30-minute low: The low is the long's version. A short's risk is above, so you use the high.
wrong.37.40, the opening price: The open is just where it started. The first 30 minutes decide the stop.
wrong.Cover now, the gap is past 2R: Not yet. The loss at 37.55 is still under 2R, so the ceiling hasn't been hit.

questions.simple: 37.55. The gap jumped the old stop, so the first 30 minutes set the new one, and on a short that's the high.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B20, mirrored for a short)

questions.q: Your short is working, and it rallies back up to the falling averages. That's a good spot to add.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. Adding is never the plan. We take the full size at one price with one stop. The size came from that stop before you got in. Add more after it moves and the position outgrows your plan. A stop-out then costs more than you meant to risk. The rare add to a winner comes on strength, as a feel call, and a rally against you isn't strength. If the crossback looks good on its own, it's a new trade with its own stop and its own size.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop. The crossback is a new trade or nothing.
questions.simple: False. Adding makes the trade bigger than your stop allowed, so we go full size once, with one stop.

deeper.counter: Kell's page offers the crossback as a place to add to the short, with a clear area to set a stop against. We use that area as the stop for a new trade instead.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, over a web view)

questions.story: Mid-morning, the stock trades down through both EMAs and through its stall low. The stall checked out, and it's under its 200-day.
questions.q: How do you get in?
choices: Short at market as it breaks
A limit order well above the market
Wait for the close, then short
Short it in the after-hours session
questions.answer: Short at market as it breaks
questions.why: Short it at market as it trades through. That's the trigger, and every setup we trade, long or short, enters right there. Not at the close. Wait for the close and the stock can be well below your trigger by then. Your stop stays over the high, so the distance grows and your share count shrinks. Market orders get you filled, and we don't enter outside regular hours.
questions.lesson_line: Short as it trades through the trigger. Not at the close, not after hours.

wrong.A limit order well above the market: A limit above the market may never fill on the day that matters. We use market orders.
wrong.Wait for the close, then short: We enter as price trades through the trigger, never at the close. By then it may have run.
wrong.Short it in the after-hours session: No new entries outside regular hours. The trigger happens during the session.

questions.simple: At market, right as it breaks. Waiting lets it run away from your stop, and that shrinks your size.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57 and E58)

questions.story: A clean five-day stall breaks down through both EMAs on Monday. The company reports after Tuesday's close.
questions.q: Can you take the short?
choices: No, it reports inside 3 days
No, the stall is too short
Yes, at half the usual size
Yes, but cover before the report
questions.answer: No, it reports inside 3 days
questions.why: No. It reports tomorrow night, inside our 3-day window, and we open nothing new in there. Even a perfect drop can get gapped right over your stop on the report. Half size doesn't solve that, it just loses less. Planning to cover first doesn't either, because the rule is about the entry itself. Let the report pass. Then look for a fresh trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Report inside 3 days, no new short. Let it pass, then look again.

wrong.Yes, at half the usual size: Smaller size still puts you in front of the report. The rule is no new short.
wrong.Yes, but cover before the report: The rule bars the entry in those 3 days, not just holding through the report.
wrong.No, the stall is too short: Five quiet days is a fine stall. The report is the problem.

questions.simple: No. It reports in less than 3 days, and a report can gap it right over your stop.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22, 3 days against 3 sessions)

questions.q: Your Wedge Drop short is working. When does the stop come down to breakeven?
choices: From 2R to 5R, or at the first sell
The day after entry, to be safe
Never, the stop stays where you set it
At 1R, once it's paid a little
questions.answer: From 2R to 5R, or at the first sell
questions.why: Somewhere from 2R to 5R, or when you make your first sell. That's a judgment, not a fixed spot. Breakeven means the trade can't turn into a loser anymore. Move it too early and normal wiggles stop you out of a short that was working fine. Wait until the trade has paid you. Then protect it. The stop only ever moves in your favor.
questions.lesson_line: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. A judgment, not a fixed day.

wrong.The day after entry, to be safe: Too early. The trade hasn't paid yet, and a normal bounce takes you out.
wrong.Never, the stop stays where you set it: The stop can move in your favor. It just never moves wider.
wrong.At 1R, once it's paid a little: Still too early. We start thinking about it at 2R.

questions.simple: Between 2R and 5R, or at the first sell. By then it has paid you, so protect it.

reasons: the breakeven range comes from the card

questions.story: Three weeks after a market low the index is still weak. A stock bounces, stalls three days and closes under both averages at 52.58.
questions.q: What risk does our card name here?
choices: Early in a new bull market
The stall is too long for a drop
The stop is too far
The volume is too light
questions.answer: Early in a new bull market
questions.why: Early in a new bull market. Our card says no short early in a new bull market, in a strongly uptrending stock, or too late in the fall. TraderLion warns the same way. In the real GOOGL case on 2019-01-14, three weeks after the December 2018 low, the short was stopped the next session at 0R. The stock was 7.2% above the entry 20 sessions later.
questions.lesson_line: A few weeks off a market low, the bounce is the trend. Do not short it.

wrong.The stall is too long for a drop: Three days is inside the 3 to 10 the card allows.
wrong.The stop is too far: GOOGL's stop was 2.1% away, inside 3%. The distance was fine; the timing was not.
wrong.The volume is too light: Volume grades the day. The risk the card names is the new bull market.

questions.simple: The card warns against shorting early in a new bull market, because the bounce can keep going.

deeper.trap: The index still looked weak: QQQ was under its 50-day on GOOGL's trigger day. But it was only three weeks after the December 2018 low. A weak-looking market does not make it safe to short early in a new bull market.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed criteria and dated example numbers

questions.q: If the honest stop over the trigger day's high is 5% away, you pull it in to 3% to fit.
questions.answer: False
questions.why: False. If the stop over the trigger day's high is more than about 3% away, you skip the trade or take the smaller size the rules give. You never pull it in. Stop first. The size comes from the stop.
questions.lesson_line: You never pick a size and back-fit a stop inside the noise.
questions.simple: False. If the honest stop is more than about 3% away, we skip the trade or size down, and we never pull the stop in.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and A13)

questions.story: Your short closed Thursday up 2.7R. Friday it gaps down and opens at 3.5R.
questions.q: What about your first cover?
choices: Judge it, 3R isn't a cover order
Cover a third at the open
Cover the whole position right now
Add more, the gap confirms it
questions.answer: Judge it, 3R isn't a cover order
questions.why: Judge it. Nothing says you cover at 3R. A gap your way is strength, and selling some into strength can make sense. It can also be the start of a bigger leg. Most of the time I'd rather sell into a 3, 5 or 7 day push than react to one open. A fixed order cuts a winner that keeps running. What you don't do is add because it gapped. Adding to a winner is rare, a feel call, never the plan.
questions.lesson_line: A gap past 3R isn't an order. It's a judgment call.

wrong.Cover a third at the open: A fixed third at 3R isn't the rule. The first cover is your judgment.
wrong.Cover the whole position right now: Nothing says a gap means cover it all. That can cut a winner short.
wrong.Add more, the gap confirms it: A gap isn't a reason to get bigger. Full size went in once, at one price, and the rare add is a feel call.

questions.simple: Your call. A gap your way is strength and you can sell some, but no rule makes you.

reasons: rests on the owner's ruling D-013 (the first sell is a judgment)
the short side mirrors the long side (D47)

questions.story: Trigger day. An 8-day stall 9.6% wide just broke under both EMAs. The stop over today's high is 2.4% away. The grade is our call on how clean a setup is, and it sets the size.
questions.q: How does that loose stall change the trade?
choices: It grades lower, and size follows
It kills the trade, wide is a no
Full grade, a 2.4% stop is tight
It raises the grade, more room to fall
questions.answer: It grades lower, and size follows
questions.why: It grades lower, and the size comes down with it. A good stall is tight. Price sits right on the averages because buyers are drying up. A 9.6% range over 8 days is loose and sloppy. Look at the 200-day too. It's still pointed up, and I want it falling for a short. That's not a no-trade, it's a lower grade, so less size. And don't let the 2.4% stop fool you. A tight stop doesn't make a messy setup clean. DXCM got stopped out by one more push up.
questions.lesson_line: A wide, loose stall grades the trade down. A tight stop doesn't fix it.

wrong.It kills the trade, wide is a no: Wide and loose lowers the grade. It doesn't cancel the trade.
wrong.Full grade, a 2.4% stop is tight: The stop distance and the stall's quality are two different things. A tight stop doesn't fix a sloppy rest.
wrong.It raises the grade, more room to fall: Loose action is messier, not better. Room to fall isn't a grade.

questions.simple: Lower grade, smaller size. A sloppy rest is less clean, and a tight stop doesn't fix that.

deeper.trap: DXCM's stop was only 2.4% away and still got taken at 0R by a 124.00 high. Then the stock fell 32.5% in 20 sessions. Right direction, stopped anyway.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
fixed before (cold check)

questions.q: An index closes 5% over its 10-day EMA. By Kell's own note, what is that?
choices: An extension; price is stretched
A healthy trend; nothing to do yet
A Wedge Drop, already confirmed
A Wedge Pop, buy the breakout
questions.answer: An extension; price is stretched
questions.why: An extension; price is stretched. Kell called QQQ a little ahead of itself at 4-5% above its daily 10-day EMA on February 2nd. We use the 9 and 20 EMA. The Wedge Drop came on 2/16 and 2/17. Our card sets about 4% or more over the 9 EMA for an index. The extension is the top. The drop is the close down through the averages days later.
questions.lesson_line: Far above the fast average, the rally is tired. Watch for the stall.

wrong.A healthy trend; nothing to do yet: An index 5% over its 10-day EMA is stretched, not healthy. Kell's note says so.
wrong.A Wedge Drop, already confirmed: The drop is the close back down through the averages, days after the top. A stretched index has not done that yet.
wrong.A Wedge Pop, buy the breakout: A pop is the close up through the averages out of a coil. This index is far above them.

questions.simple: Kell called an index 4 to 5 percent above its 10-day average a little ahead of itself, so 5 percent is stretched.

reasons: a threshold the card proposes (about 4% for an index)
fixed before (cold check)

questions.story: Same stall, two different drop days. Drop A closes mid-range on light volume. Drop B gaps down and closes at its low on heavy volume. The grade is our call on how clean it is, and it sets the size.
questions.q: Which one grades higher?
choices: Drop B, sellers ran it all day
Drop A, quiet is better
Same grade, only the EMAs matter
Drop A, more room left to fall
questions.answer: Drop B, sellers ran it all day
questions.why: Drop B. A gap down that closes right at its low means sellers had it the whole day. Nobody stepped in. That's the kind of drop I want to short. Drop A closing mid-range is a shrug, with buyers and sellers splitting the day. The heavy volume helps too. It raises the grade, but it's not a must. Grading is still a judgment, and B just looks cleaner.
questions.lesson_line: A drop that closes at its low shows real sellers. That raises the grade.

wrong.Drop A, quiet is better: Quiet is what you want in the stall. On the drop day you want sellers showing up.
wrong.Same grade, only the EMAs matter: The EMAs are the trigger. Where the day closes and who's selling still shape the grade.
wrong.Drop A, more room left to fall: A mid-range close is the weaker day. Light volume doesn't leave more room to fall.

questions.simple: Drop B. Closing at the low after a gap down shows sellers ran the whole day.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-006, trigger volume)

deeper.counter: In our own scan, heavy volume on the drop day raised the win rate but not the average R. So it's a plus, never a must.

questions.q: Our card prefers a 200-day that is lower than it was 20 sessions ago.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. The card prefers a falling 200-day: lower than it was 20 sessions ago. It is a preference, not a gate. The gate is a close under the 200-day. WHR's August 2002 drop came under a falling 200-day, in a bear market.
questions.lesson_line: Under a falling 200-day the trend is on your side. Prefer it.
questions.simple: True. We prefer a 200-day average that is lower than it was 20 sessions ago, because the bigger trend is down.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

If the stop hits, you lose about the $500 you planned. That's the whole point of sizing off the stop. The stop sits 2.71% away, inside what we like, so the size is honest.
questions.lesson_line: Dollars at risk divided by the distance to the stop. Round down.
questions.simple: 140 shares. Your dollar risk divided by the risk on each share, rounded down.

184 shares
140 shares
1,404 shares

wrong.184 shares: That's $500 divided by the stop's percent, not by the dollars a share.
