questions.story: You short the trigger day at 131.23 with the stop at 134.79.
You're short from 52.58 with the stop at 53.70. The next session trades up through 53.70 and closes at 54.33.
questions.q: Where did the trade end?
choices: At 53.70, a planned loss
Still short, the stop needs a close
At the close, 54.33
Stopped, so re-short right away
questions.answer: At 53.70, a planned loss
questions.why: At 53.70. Your stop is a real order with the broker, and it filled the moment price traded through. That's a planned loss, exactly the size you sized for. The 54.33 close is where you'd be with no stop in, a bigger loss. That's why the stop sits with the broker and not in your head. GOOGL did this three weeks after the December 2018 low, with QQQ still under its 50-day.
questions.lesson_line: The stop is the exit. It fills where you put it, not at the close.

wrong.Still short, the stop needs a close: A stop is an order, not a close you wait on. It filled at 53.70.
wrong.At the close, 54.33: The stop went during the day at 53.70. The close is only where you'd be without one.
wrong.Stopped, so re-short right away: After a stop-out, a new short needs a new trigger and its own stop.

questions.simple: At 53.70. The stop is a real order, so it filled there and capped the loss you planned.

deeper.trap: The close at 54.33 is not your exit price. Waiting for a close back under 53.70 turns a planned loss into a larger one. The stop is the exit.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4)

questions.story: This is an index fund, name hidden. It wedge dropped a few days ago. Now it's rallied back up to its falling averages and stalled right under them.
questions.q: What's that rally?
choices: A crossback, a retest of the EMAs
A new Wedge Drop, a second short
A Wedge Pop, a buy signal
A reclaim, the drop has failed
questions.answer: A crossback, a retest of the EMAs
questions.why: A crossback. After a drop, price often rallies back to retest the averages. This one closed under them again. Look at the last candle though. It's a hammer, a long lower wick and a close near the high. Buyers showed up during the day, so stay alert. If you're short, sit tight and let the trail cover you on a close back above them. What you don't do is add here. If it looks good on its own, that's a new trade with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: The first rally back into falling averages is normal. Hold, and let the trail decide.

wrong.A new Wedge Drop, a second short: A second drop needs a new stall and a new close down through both. This one's a rally back up.
wrong.A Wedge Pop, a buy signal: A pop closes up through both averages from under them. This one stalled underneath.
wrong.A reclaim, the drop has failed: Failed means a close back above both averages. This rally stalled under them.

questions.simple: A crossback. It's a retest that stalls under the falling averages, so a short holds and doesn't add.

deeper.trap: Kell's own QQQ run went extension, then the Wedge Drop, then the EMA Crossback. His page offers the crossback as a place to add to the short. We don't add on a rally against us: one price, one stop.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
tied to a held decision (D-002)

questions.q: This short grades A+, our cleanest. But it's hard to borrow and the fee is high. What do you do?
choices: Skip it, the borrow comes first
Skip it, the chart is stretched
Short it at half size
Short it, an A+ chart wins
questions.answer: Skip it, the borrow comes first
questions.why: Skip it. We pass on any short that's hard to borrow or carries a high fee, no matter how good the chart looks. You pay that fee every day you're in. And a hard-to-borrow stock may not stay available to you. Half size doesn't change any of that. A great chart can't fix a bad borrow.
questions.lesson_line: If you can't borrow it cleanly, it's not a short. Skip it.

wrong.Short it at half size: Half of a hard borrow is still a hard borrow.
wrong.Skip it, the chart is stretched: Nothing says the chart is stretched. It's an A+. The borrow is the problem.
wrong.Short it, an A+ chart wins: The borrow comes before the chart. A+ only says how clean the chart is.

questions.simple: Skip it. The fee costs you every day and the borrow can go away, so the chart can't save it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D48)

questions.q: A blow-off top shorted on its climax day above the 200-day is the Parabolic Short's trade, not a Wedge Drop.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. A short above the 200-day after a blow-off is the Parabolic Short, taken on its climax day with its own checklist. The Wedge Drop comes days later, after a stall within 1 ATR of the 10-day EMA. Bracco's target for the Parabolic Short is the 9-day EMA, which acts as a magnet for mean reversion.
questions.lesson_line: Shorting the blow-off is a different setup. The Wedge Drop comes days later, back at the averages.
questions.simple: True. Shorting a blow-off on its climax day is the Parabolic Short, and a Wedge Drop comes days later.

deeper.counter: Timing separates the two. A Parabolic Short is the climax day of a 3 to 5 day burst, 10% or more over the 9-day EMA. A Wedge Drop needs the stall first, then the close through the averages.

reasons: +2 rests on a held decision (D-040, the parabolic exception)

questions.story: A stock in an uptrend bounces, stalls on its averages and closes under both. The close is 8.3% above its 200-day.
questions.q: What is it for us?
choices: A sell signal for a long, not a short
An A+ short
A Wedge Pop
A parabolic short
questions.answer: A sell signal for a long, not a short
questions.why: A sell signal, not a short. Shorts only below the 200-day. V 2021-05-10 was this, above the 200-day in an uptrend. The short ran 0.93R and was stopped.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day the drop tells a long holder to sell. It gives a short seller nothing.

wrong.An A+ short: No short above the 200-day, however clean the stall. That is a hard rule.
wrong.A Wedge Pop: A pop closes up through the averages. This closed down through them.
wrong.A parabolic short: A parabolic short is a climax day after a 3 to 5 day burst. This is a stall and a drop.

questions.story: The trigger day is the last bar. In the stall, one close sits more than 1 ATR from the 9 EMA. Then the stock closes under both averages.
questions.q: Does that pass our stall test?
choices: No; one close was past 1 ATR
Yes; the stall was long enough
Yes; that distance is fine
No; the stall was too short
questions.answer: No; one close was past 1 ATR
questions.why: No. Through the stall no close is more than 1 ATR from the 9 EMA. One close past 1 ATR fails that test. The stall's length is inside the 3 to 10 the card allows, so length is not the problem. The 1 ATR is the card's proposed number. WFC was this near miss: an extension turn with no real stall, the mean-reversion short and not a Wedge Drop.
questions.lesson_line: Count the quiet days. One close too far from the 9 EMA and it is not a stall.

wrong.Yes; the stall was long enough: Length is one test. The distance is another, and one close failed it.
wrong.No; the stall was too short: The stall's length is inside the 3 to 10 sessions the card allows. The distance is what fails.
wrong.Yes; that distance is fine: The card says no close is more than 1 ATR from the 9 EMA. This one is past it.

questions.simple: No. One close past 1 ATR from the 9 EMA breaks the stall test, even when the stall is long enough.

deeper.trap: One stretched close breaks a stall. A close that far from the 9 EMA means the move is still extended with no real stall, so it is not a Wedge Drop.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: Trigger day. Through the stall, the up days ran 2.84 times the volume of the down days. Then a close under both EMAs.
questions.q: What was really going on in that stall?
choices: Accumulation, buyers were still there
A clean stall, the up days were quiet
Distribution, sellers were in charge
Exhaustion, the buyers were all spent
questions.answer: Accumulation, buyers were still there
questions.why: Accumulation. Somebody was buying. In a clean stall the volume dries up on the up days, because new buyers are running out. Here the up days ran 2.84 times the volume of the down days. That's the opposite. Buyers kept stepping in, so the rest wasn't over. That makes it a weak short, and VZ proved it. It rallied back through the averages and took the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy up days in the stall mean someone's buying. That's a weak short.

wrong.A clean stall, the up days were quiet: The up days were 2.84 times heavier than the down days. That's not quiet.
wrong.Distribution, sellers were in charge: Heavy up days mean buyers. Distribution is heavy selling.
wrong.Exhaustion, the buyers were all spent: Spent buyers show up as quiet up days. These were loud.

questions.simple: Buyers were still stepping in, so the rest wasn't over and the short was weak.

deeper.trap: The close under both averages is only one gate. The stall's volume is another, and here it failed. VZ looked like a Wedge Drop on the chart, ran 0.54R, then was stopped as the stock rallied through the averages.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review

questions.story: Fifth straight up day. The stock is 25% over its 9 EMA. It gaps up, then closes red.
questions.q: Which setup is this?
choices: A Parabolic Short, the climax day
A Wedge Drop after a quiet stall
A Wedge Pop out of a tight coil
A downside crossback, a retest
questions.answer: A Parabolic Short, the climax day
questions.why: The Parabolic Short. It's a blow-off: five straight up days, 25% over the 9 EMA, then a gap up that closes red. That's the climax day. A Wedge Drop is a different animal. It comes later, after price has come back and rested on its averages. Name the setup first, because the plans are different. My target on a parabolic short is the 9 EMA, which acts like a magnet.
questions.lesson_line: Check the distance to the averages. Far above them on a climax day is the other setup.

wrong.A downside crossback, a retest: A crossback is a rally back into the averages after a drop. Nothing has dropped yet.
wrong.A Wedge Drop after a quiet stall: There's no stall on the averages. Price is way above them.
wrong.A Wedge Pop out of a tight coil: A pop closes up through the averages out of a coil. Here it's a blow-off far above them.

questions.simple: A Parabolic Short. It's a climax far above the 9 EMA, not a drop out of a rest on the averages.

deeper.trap: Distance is the tell. A Wedge Drop stalls on its averages. A Parabolic Short sits far above its 9 EMA after a burst of up days. The same red close can show up in both, one at the averages and the other far above them.

reasons: rests on a proposed card criterion awaiting owner review
tied to a held decision (D-040)

questions.story: For two weeks price coiled under both EMAs. Today it closed up through both.
questions.q: What setup just triggered?
choices: A Wedge Pop, the mirror setup
A Wedge Drop, a sell signal
A downside crossback, a test
An upside crossback, a test
questions.answer: A Wedge Pop, the mirror setup
questions.why: A Wedge Pop. Look at where price came from and which way it closed. It sat under both averages and closed up through them. That's the pop, a buy setup. A Wedge Drop is the mirror: it rests on or above them and closes down through them. Same two lines, opposite sides. A cross alone doesn't name the setup. Where it rested does.
questions.lesson_line: Same averages, opposite sides. Where it rested and which way it closed tell you which.

wrong.A Wedge Drop, a sell signal: A drop closes down through the averages from on or above them. This closed up from below.
wrong.A downside crossback, a test: A downside crossback stalls under falling averages. This went right through them.
wrong.An upside crossback, a test: A crossback is a retest. Here it's the first close up through both.

questions.simple: A Wedge Pop. Price coiled under the averages and closed up through them, the mirror of a drop.

deeper.trap: A close through the averages is not enough to name the setup. Which side price came from decides it. Coiled under and closed up through both is the Pop. Stalled on or above and closed down through both is the Drop. Kell also warns the pop is not simply a cross, since price bars and volume matter.

reasons: tied to a held decision (D-078)

questions.q: An intraday break of the stall low on the 65-minute chart counts only once the daily close confirms it.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Kell says hourly and 15-minute charts are for timing entries. Our card counts a break of the stall low on the 65-minute chart only once the daily close confirms it. The daily close is the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: The hourly chart can sharpen the entry. The daily close is still the judge.
questions.simple: True. The hourly break can help time the entry, but our card counts it only after the daily close confirms it.

deeper.trap: Shorting inside the stall before the close confirms is a named mistake. An intraday break of the stall low is only a hint until the daily close confirms it. The drop is a one-day event that the next day confirms or cancels.

reasons: rests on a proposed advanced card rule

questions.q: The 9 EMA is 40.00 and the stock opens at 36.40. How far under the average is the open, in percent?
questions.why: 9.0%. The open is under the average by (40.00 - 36.40) / 40.00 x 100 = 9.0%. That is under 10%, so this test does not stop the short at that open. We skip a short more than 10% under its 9 EMA, checked at the open on a gap down.
questions.lesson_line: Check the stretch at the open on a gap down. Past 10% under the 9 EMA, pass.
questions.simple: Take the average minus the open and divide by the average. That is 9.0%, under the 10% line, so this test lets the short through.

deeper.trap: Divide by the average, not by the open. The average is the line the open sits under. Use average minus open, over average.

reasons: +2 a computed key

wrong.9.9%: Divided by the open, not by the average.
wrong.3.6%: Used the dollar gap as if it were the percent.
wrong.0.9%: A decimal slip. The open is far more than one percent under the average.

questions.story: A failed-push top, a three-day stall, a drop on 3.3x volume. You shorted at 24.74, stop 25.26. It never passes 0.34R; on day 8 the stop is hit.
questions.q: Was that loss a mistake?
choices: No; a planned loss, the stop worked
No; you should have covered at 0.34R
Yes; 3.3x volume said stay out
Yes; the stop was far too tight
questions.answer: No; a planned loss, the stop worked
questions.why: No. A stop hit is the plan working. The stop is the exit and is never widened. This one sat 2.1% over the 24.74 fill, inside the 3% a stop usually stays within. The trade peaked at 0.34R and was stopped on day 8. Volume on the drop does not change what a stop-out is.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working. You will take this one again.

wrong.Yes; the stop was far too tight: It sat 2.1% over the fill, inside the usual 3%, and it held until day 8.
wrong.No; you should have covered at 0.34R: Nothing in the plan covers at 0.34R. The first cover is a third at 3R, and the stop is the exit.
wrong.Yes; 3.3x volume said stay out: Volume on the drop grades the day. It does not make a stop-out at plan a mistake.

questions.simple: No. A stop hit is the plan working, because the stop is the exit and the loss was the one we planned.

deeper.trap: A loss is not a mistake just because the setup failed. Judge the trade against the plan: stop first, stop respected, never widened. This trade reached only 0.34R before the stop. That is how a stop works, not a breach of the plan.

reasons: +2 rests on a held decision (D-006, trigger volume)
+1 fixed before

questions.story: You were long. It closed down through both EMAs, so you sold. Two days later it closes back above both and takes off.
questions.q: Now what?
choices: Nothing, buy only on a new setup
Buy it back now, it was a shakeout
Short it, it'll fail again
Wait a few days, then buy it back
questions.answer: Nothing, buy only on a new setup
questions.why: Nothing yet. Selling was right. The drop is the last exit on a long, and you took it. Some of these get taken back fast. In our scan, 38.2% closed back above both averages within 3 sessions. That's the cost of having an exit. Don't chase it back in because it feels like a mistake. Buy it again when a new setup triggers, with its own stop.
questions.lesson_line: A shakeout isn't a buy signal. The next setup is.

wrong.Wait a few days, then buy it back: A clock isn't a trigger. Buy again when the setup triggers again.
wrong.Buy it back now, it was a shakeout: Knowing it was a shakeout isn't a trigger. You need a setup and a stop.
wrong.Short it, it'll fail again: It just took back both averages. Shorting that is fighting strength with no setup.

questions.simple: Nothing yet. Selling was right, and you buy back only when a new setup gives you a stop.

deeper.trap: The hindsight trap is feeling that selling was a mistake because it reclaimed and ran. The rule did not change. Selling at the drop was the plan, and getting back in is a new decision with a new stop. Shorting the reclaim is the opposite error, fighting a stock that just took back both averages.

reasons: a card rule built on the settled re-entry rule

questions.story: Trigger day. The stall breaks on a gap down and everything else checks out. Your fill is 90.85 and the stop over the high is 93.53, 3.0% away.
questions.q: Do you take it?
choices: Yes, 3.0% is a fair stop
No, never short a gap down
Yes, but pull the stop to 2%
No, anything past 2% is a pass
questions.answer: Yes, 3.0% is a fair stop
questions.why: Yes. We like stops 1 to 3% away, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% is fine. 3.0% sits right in there. A slightly wider stop just means fewer shares for the same risk. What you never do is pull the stop in to fit more size. Then it's inside the day's range, and one more push up takes you out. TSM hit 3R on day 9 and reached 6.4R at best.
questions.lesson_line: A 3% stop is fine. Never pull a stop in to fit.

wrong.Yes, but pull the stop to 2%: Never pull the stop in to fit. It goes over the high, or you skip.
wrong.No, never short a gap down: A gap down through the stall low is a fine trigger. The only question here is the stop.
wrong.No, anything past 2% is a pass: We prefer 1 to 3% and accept up to 5%. 3.0% is fine.

questions.simple: Yes. 3.0% is inside what we accept, and a wider stop just means fewer shares.

deeper.trap: The trap is the fix. If the stop were past 5%, we would mostly wait for a tighter trigger. We never pull the stop in to make it fit. Here nothing needs fixing: 3.0% is inside the 1 to 3% we prefer.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.story: Ten sessions after you shorted, the trade is up 1.4R and drifting sideways on the averages.
questions.q: Hold it or cover it?
choices: Hold, it's past the 1R bar
Cover, ten sessions is the limit
Cover, it's stopped moving
Add on a pop to the averages
questions.answer: Hold, it's past the 1R bar
questions.why: Hold. The time stop is for trades that did nothing, still under 1R after 10 trading days. Those get closed so the money can go somewhere better. This one is up 1.4R. It's done something. Let the stop, your covers and the trail run it from here.
questions.lesson_line: Under 1R after ten days, it's out. Past 1R, let your other rules run it.

wrong.Add on a pop to the averages: A pop against you is no place to add. Full size at one price, one stop.
wrong.Cover, ten sessions is the limit: Ten sessions only matters for a trade still under 1R. This one is past it.
wrong.Cover, it's stopped moving: Drifting isn't the rule. Under 1R after 10 sessions is.

questions.simple: Hold. The time stop is for trades that did nothing, and this one is up 1.4R.

deeper.trap: Reading the rule as 'ten days and out' is the slip. The bar is 1R of profit, and 1.4R clears it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.story: The company reported last night. Today, after a six-day stall on the averages, it gaps down and closes under both, near its low.
questions.q: Does the earnings rule block this short?
choices: No; the reaction day is allowed
Yes; no shorts near earnings
Yes; wait 3 sessions post-report
No; earnings only blocks longs
questions.answer: No; the reaction day is allowed
questions.why: No. The rule is no new short in the 3 sessions before a report. The reason is the overnight gap, which a stop cannot catch. Once the report is out that risk is over, so a Wedge Drop that is the earnings reaction itself is allowed. The report here came last night, so the sessions before it are over.
questions.lesson_line: Before the report, wait. The reaction day can be the drop.

wrong.Yes; no shorts near earnings: The rule bars new shorts in the 3 sessions before a report. This report is already out.
wrong.Yes; wait 3 sessions post-report: There is no waiting period after a report. The gap through the averages is the trigger.
wrong.No; earnings only blocks longs: The 3-session rule covers new shorts too. It is the report being over that frees this one.

questions.simple: No. The rule guards against the gap before a report, and this report is already out.

deeper.trap: There are two ways to get this wrong. One is shorting in the 3 sessions before the report, which the rule bars. The other is treating the reaction day as blocked too. The rule counts the 3 sessions before a report, not the days after it. The other gates still apply, so the drop still needs its stall and its close under both averages.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook

questions.q: You're hunting Wedge Drop shorts. What RS rating are you looking for?
choices: 20 or less, in a weak group
80 or more, in a strong group
Any rating, the chart decides
50 or less, in a weak group
questions.answer: 20 or less, in a weak group
questions.why: 20 or less, in a weak group. A short is buying leaders flipped around. You want the weakest stocks in the weakest groups. An RS rating of 20 or less means it's lagging most of the market. Short a strong stock and it tends to bounce right through your stop. Check the RS rating before you short anything. We're extremely picky with shorts, maybe one or two a cycle.
questions.lesson_line: Short the weakest in the weakest groups. The mirror of buying leaders.

wrong.80 or more, in a strong group: That's the leader side, the stocks we buy.
wrong.Any rating, the chart decides: The chart is one check. Weakness is another.
wrong.50 or less, in a weak group: The line is 20 or less. A 50 is the middle of the pack.

questions.simple: 20 or less, in a weak group. Weak stocks keep falling, and strong ones bounce through your stop.

deeper.trap: RS of 20 or less is a gate, not a trigger. The stock also needs the 200-day, the market reading, the stall and the close through the averages. We are extremely picky: one or two shorts per cycle.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C31, the short mirror)

questions.story: The trigger was 64.63. You were away from the screen when it broke. Next morning it opens at 61.50.
questions.q: Short it at the open?
choices: No, it's over 4% past the trigger
Yes, the drop's confirmed, take it
Yes, at half the usual size
No, never short at the open
questions.answer: No, it's over 4% past the trigger
questions.why: No. 61.50 is more than 4% under 64.63, and we don't chase past 4%. That's the same no-chasing rule we use on buys, flipped. Your stop still belongs over the trigger day's high, so the distance just got bigger. Same risk, bigger distance, fewer shares. You'd be taking a worse trade at a smaller size. You missed it. That happens. Wait for the next one.
questions.lesson_line: More than 4% past the trigger, let it go. There's always another one.

wrong.Yes, at half the usual size: Half of a chase is still a chase.
wrong.Yes, the drop's confirmed, take it: It is confirmed. It's also too far gone. The chase line is 4%.
wrong.No, never short at the open: Opening under the trigger can be fine. Here it's just too far under.

questions.simple: No. It opened more than 4% past the trigger, so you'd be chasing with a smaller size.

deeper.trap: The 4% line is measured from the trigger level, not from where you wish you had filled. Being away from the screen does not open a wider window. A later short needs a new stall and a new close under both averages.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook
fixed before (cold check)

questions.story: The market filter in our app reads Red, its weakest reading: mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day. A stock under its falling 200-day pops into its 50-day, makes a lower high, stalls five days and closes under both EMAs.
questions.q: Where does that leave you?
choices: A candidate, with more checks to run
Short it right now, Red means shorts
A candidate, but Red blocks it
Sell signal only, no short
questions.answer: A candidate, with more checks to run
questions.why: A candidate. The big things line up. Red means mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day, and this stock is under a falling 200-day. It popped into the 50-day, made a lower high and failed. That's exactly the picture I want. Our scan found the drop only had an edge in spots like this. But a candidate isn't a trade yet. The stop, the borrow, the report date and the RS rating still have to pass.
questions.lesson_line: Red market, under the 200-day, a failed pop. That's a candidate. Now run the rest of the checks.

wrong.A candidate, but Red blocks it: Red doesn't block shorts. Red is mostly cash plus shorts below the 200-day.
wrong.Short it right now, Red means shorts: Red and the 200-day are two checks of several. The stop, borrow, report and RS still come first.
wrong.Sell signal only, no short: Above the 200-day it would be. Under a falling 200-day in a Red market it can be a short.

questions.simple: A candidate. The market and the 200-day allow a short, but the stop, borrow and report checks come next.

deeper.trap: A candidate is not a trade yet. The stop must be close enough to fit our stop rules. The stock must be easy to borrow. No report may fall in the next 3 sessions, and the RS rating should be 20 or less. Fail one, and it is a skip.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook and a held decision (D-023, the market filter)
+1 fixed before

questions.story: A bounce dies at the falling 50-day, then a four-day stall. Today it trades down through both EMAs and the stall low, closing at 131.23. The day's high is 134.76.
questions.q: Write the plan. Entry, stop and first cover?
choices: Through trigger, stop 134.79, day 3+
Through trigger, stop 134.79, day 1
At the close, stop 134.79, day 3+
Through trigger, stop 133.00, day 3+
questions.answer: Through trigger, stop 134.79, day 3+
questions.why: Short as it trades through the trigger, stop at 134.79, first cover on day 3 or later. Shorts get in just like buys, through the trigger and never at the close. Look at today's candle. It ran up to 134.76 and got sold all day, a long upper wick. The stop goes a few cents over that high, the closest spot that proves you wrong. From 131.23 that's about 2.7%, inside the 3% I want. Then give it a few days. GS hit 3R on day 4.
questions.lesson_line: Entry, stop, cover. Write it before it triggers, then just execute it.

wrong.Through trigger, stop 134.79, day 1: We very rarely sell on day 1. Give it room to work.
wrong.At the close, stop 134.79, day 3+: Shorts enter through the trigger, like buys. Never at the close.
wrong.Through trigger, stop 133.00, day 3+: 133.00 sits inside the day's range, under the 134.76 high. One more push takes it.

questions.simple: Short through the trigger, stop a few cents over the high, and wait until day 3 before covering any.

deeper.example: GS, 2011-08-02: the bounce died at the falling 50-day, then a four-day stall, then a close at 131.23. The stop at 134.79 was about 2.7% away. Measured from that close, 3R came on day 4. At best it reached 13.2R, a high-water mark on a fixed stop, not a result to bank.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook and the D-013 first-sell judgment
the short entry on the close is not covered by D-003

questions.story: This is an index fund, name hidden. Today, a Friday, the Nasdaq closed down through both EMAs, with the big AI names leading it lower. You hold six longs.
questions.q: What's the index telling you?
choices: Get defensive, trim some longs
Buy the dip in the big leaders
Nothing, only single stocks matter
Hold, wait for the 200-day to go
questions.answer: Get defensive, trim some longs
questions.why: Get defensive. When the index itself wedge drops, the whole market is getting weaker, and every long you hold feels it. You've got six longs exposed to that. Trim some, tighten up, cut your exposure. Your job here isn't to call the next leg down. It's to make sure you aren't fully loaded if it comes. We read this exact drop as the start of another leg down at the time.
questions.lesson_line: When the index wedge drops, your longs are on notice. Reduce first, ask later.

wrong.Buy the dip in the big leaders: Leaders falling through their averages is a reason to get defensive, not to buy.
wrong.Nothing, only single stocks matter: The index's drop is a warning for every long you own.
wrong.Hold, wait for the 200-day to go: The 200-day is a separate test for shorts. The index's drop is already the warning.

questions.simple: Get defensive. A drop in the index means the whole market is weakening, and your longs feel it.

A plan, short the 166.50 break
Short it now, then set a stop later
Ignore it, posts aren't ideas

questions.q: You're trailing the rest of a short with the 9 EMA. At noon price pokes above it, then closes back under. Cover?
choices: No, the close under it keeps you in
Yes, any trade above it is a cover
Yes, cover half and trail the rest
Yes, the poke shows buyers are back
questions.answer: No, the close under it keeps you in
questions.why: No. You're still short. We cover what's left on a close back above the trail, not on a poke. Intraday pokes happen all the time on a falling stock. React to every one and you'll get shaken out of a short that's still working. It closed back under the 9 EMA, so the trade is fine. Use the 9 EMA for fast movers and the 20 EMA for steadier ones.
questions.lesson_line: Cover on the close back above the line, not on the poke.

wrong.Yes, any trade above it is a cover: A touch isn't a close. We cover on a close above the line.
wrong.Yes, cover half and trail the rest: What's left comes off in one piece on the close above the line. A faded poke changes nothing.
wrong.Yes, the poke shows buyers are back: A poke that fades by the close is noise, not buyers taking over.

questions.simple: No. You cover on a close back above the line, and a poke that fades is just noise.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E52)

questions.q: We only recommend shorting to traders who have already made $1 million trading.
questions.answer: True
questions.why: True. Shorting is harder than buying. You need tight stops, and volatility picks up as a stock falls. So we only recommend it once you've already made $1 million trading. Until then the Wedge Drop still earns its keep. It's your sell signal on a long, and that alone saves you a lot of money.
questions.lesson_line: Shorting is for traders who've made $1 million. Everyone can use the drop as a sell signal.
questions.simple: True. Shorts are harder and need tight stops, so we recommend them only after you've made $1 million.

questions.q: What's the move here?
questions.story: Six days resting on the averages, and they're flattening out. Today is another quiet day. Price hasn't fallen through them yet.
choices: Wait until it falls through them
Short now, the top is already in
Short now, stop over the stall high
Buy it, a quiet rest means strength
questions.answer: Wait until it falls through them
questions.why: Wait. Right now it's just a rest. The drop is the day price falls through both averages, and that hasn't happened. Short inside the rest and you're guessing. One more push up and your stop's gone. I want the stall to resolve first. Then you short as price trades down through the trigger. EXP did break the next day and hit 3R in three sessions.
questions.lesson_line: A rest is only a rest. Short as it falls through, not before.
questions.simple: Wait. A rest is only a rest, so short when price actually falls through the averages.

wrong.Short now, stop over the stall high: Same mistake with a stop attached. Buyers haven't given up yet.
wrong.Short now, the top is already in: A rest isn't a drop. Short early and one more push up takes your stop.
wrong.Buy it, a quiet rest means strength: A quiet rest under a top isn't strength. Buyers are thinning out.

questions.q: Does the light volume kill the setup?
questions.story: The last day of 2025, a holiday week. A tight stall, then a drop on light holiday volume, 0.4 times normal. Everything else checks out. The grade is our call on how clean it is, and it sets the size.
choices: No, volume only adds to the grade
Yes, a drop needs heavy volume
Yes, light volume means no sellers
No, but cut the size in half
questions.answer: No, volume only adds to the grade
questions.why: No. Volume raises the grade. It's not a must. What shows you sellers took over is price falling through both averages and the stall low. Heavy volume would've been a plus. Light holiday volume just means no bonus. Holiday weeks are thin for everybody, so don't read much into it. GEN went on to reach 18.0R at best.
questions.lesson_line: Heavy volume raises the grade. A drop on light volume still counts.
questions.simple: No. Volume only adds to the grade, so a drop on light volume still counts.

wrong.Yes, a drop needs heavy volume: Volume raises the grade. It isn't a requirement.
wrong.Yes, light volume means no sellers: Price falling through both averages and the stall low shows the sellers. Volume is a bonus.
wrong.No, but cut the size in half: There's no halving rule for light volume. It just earns no bonus.
